column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 37: The writing of good and bad deeds

column2: From Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in what he relates from his Lord, Blessed and Exalted is He, who said: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has written down the good deeds and the bad deeds, then He made that clear. Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it,

Allah writes it down with Him as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it down with Him as ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times, up to many times more. If he intends a bad deed and does not do it, He writes it down with Him as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it down as a single bad deed.”
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim reported it.
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of al-Jaʿd Abū ʿUthmān: Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī told us, from Ibn ʿAbbās.
A narration of Muslim's has an addition at the end of the hadith: “or Allah erases it; and none perishes before Allah except one who is doomed to perish.”

There are many hadiths with this meaning. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah says: When My servant wants to do a bad deed, do not write it against him until he does it. If he does it,

write it as one like it; and if he leaves it for My sake, write it for him as a good deed. When he wants to do a good deed and does not do it, write it for him as a good deed; and if he does it, write it for him as ten like it, up to seven hundred times.” This is al-Bukhārī's wording. In a narration of Muslim's:
“Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: When My servant talks of doing a good deed, I write it for him as a good deed so long as he has not done it; and when he does it,
I write it as ten like it. When he talks of doing a bad deed, I forgive it for him so long as he has not done it; and when he does it, I write it for him as one like it.”

And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “The angels said: My Lord, that servant of Yours wants to do a bad deed — though He sees him better than they do. He said: Watch him. If he does it, write it for him as one like it; and if he leaves it, write it for him as a good deed; he left it only for My sake.”

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “When one of you makes his Islam excellent, every good deed he does is written as ten like it, up to seven hundred times, and every bad deed he does is written as one like it, until he meets Allah.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Every deed of the son of Ādam is multiplied: a good deed is ten like it, up to seven hundred times. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: Except fasting, for it is Mine,
and I reward it; he leaves his desire, his food and his drink for My sake.” In one narration, after his words “up to seven hundred times”, there is: “up to whatever Allah wills.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Dharr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah says: Whoever does a good deed will have ten like it, or I will give more; and whoever does a bad deed, its recompense is one like it, or I will forgive.”
It also has, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, a good deed is written for him;
and if he does it, ten are written for him. Whoever intends a bad deed and does not do it, nothing is written against him; and if he does it, a single bad deed is written against him.”

In the Musnad, from Khuraym ibn Fātik, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, and Allah knows that he has let his heart feel it and was eager for it, a good deed is written for him.

Whoever intends a bad deed, it is not written against him; and whoever does it, a single one is written against him and it is not multiplied against him. Whoever does a good deed will have ten like it, and whoever spends something in the path of Allah will have it seven hundred times over.”
There are many other hadiths with this meaning.
These texts, then, cover the writing of good deeds and bad deeds, and of intending a good deed and a bad deed. These are four kinds.

The first kind is doing good deeds. A good deed is multiplied tenfold, up to seven hundred times, up to many times more. Multiplying a good deed tenfold applies to every good deed without exception; it is shown by His words, Exalted is He: “Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten like it” [al-Anʿām 6:160].
As for multiplying beyond ten for whomever Allah wills, that is shown by His words, Exalted is He:

“The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the path of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains; and Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing” [al-Baqarah 2:261]. This verse shows that spending in the path of Allah is multiplied seven hundred times.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Masʿūd, who said: A man brought a she-camel with a halter and said: Messenger of Allah, this is for the path of Allah. He said: “For it you will have seven hundred she-camels on the Day of Resurrection.”
In the Musnad, with a chain open to question, from Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever spends something over and above in the path of Allah has it seven hundred times over; and whoever spends on himself and his family, or visits a sick person, or removes something harmful, the good deed is ten like it.”

Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Muʿādh, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Prayer, fasting and remembrance are multiplied seven hundred times over spending in the path of Allah.”
Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, with his chain of narration, from al-Ḥasan, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever sends money to be spent in the path of Allah and stays at home

has for every dirham seven hundred dirhams; and whoever goes on campaign himself in the path of Allah has for every dirham seven hundred thousand dirhams.” Then he recited this verse: “And Allah multiplies for whom He wills” [al-Baqarah 2:261].

Ibn Ḥibbān recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of ʿĪsā ibn al-Musayyab, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: When this verse came down, “The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the path of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts seven ears” [al-Baqarah 2:261],

the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “My Lord, give my nation more.” So Allah the Exalted sent down: “Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan, that He may multiply it for him many times over?” [al-Baqarah 2:245]. He said: “My Lord, give my nation more.” So Allah the Exalted sent down: “Only the patient will be paid their reward in full, without measure” [al-Zumar 39:10].
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of ʿAlī ibn Zayd ibn Judʿān, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ
said: “Allah multiplies a good deed to two million good deeds.” Then Abū Hurayrah recited: “And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:40].
And he said: “When Allah says ‘a great reward’, who can measure it?”
It is also narrated from Abū Hurayrah as mawqūf (his own words).

Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ): “Whoever enters the market and says, ‘There is no god but Allah alone, without partner; His is the dominion and His the praise; He gives life and causes death,

and He is Ever-Living and does not die; in His hand is all good, and He has power over all things,’ Allah writes for him a million good deeds, erases from him a million bad deeds, and raises him a million degrees.”
And from the hadith of Tamīm al-Dārī, as marfūʿ: “Whoever says, ‘I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, One God, Unique, Self-Sufficient,
who has taken neither wife nor son, and to whom none is equal,’ ten times, Allah writes for him forty million good deeds.” Both chains contain weakness.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a weak chain, from Ibn ʿUmar, as marfūʿ: “Whoever says subḥān Allāh, Allah writes for him a hundred and twenty-four thousand good deeds.”

His words in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, “Except fasting, for it is Mine, and I reward it,” show that none but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows how far the reward of fasting is multiplied, because it is the best kind of patience,
and “Only the patient will be paid their reward in full, without measure” [al-Zumar 39:10]. This meaning has been narrated from a group of the Salaf, among them Kaʿb and others.

We mentioned earlier, in the commentary on the hadith, “Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him,” that the multiplying of good deeds beyond ten depends on the excellence of one's Islam,
as is stated explicitly in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah and others; and it depends on the perfection of one's sincerity, on the merit of the deed itself, and on how much it is needed.

We also mentioned, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, that His words, “Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten like it” [al-Anʿām 6:160], came down concerning the Bedouins, and that His words, “And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward” [al-Nisāʾ 4:40], came down concerning the Emigrants.

The second kind is doing bad deeds. A bad deed is written as one like it, without multiplication, as the Exalted says: “And whoever comes with a bad deed will be recompensed only with its like, and they will not be wronged” [al-Anʿām 6:160].

His words, “a single bad deed is written for him,” indicate that it is not multiplied, which is stated explicitly in another hadith. A bad deed may, however, become graver because of the sanctity of the time or the place, as the Exalted says:

“The number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of these, four are sacred. That is the upright religion, so do not wrong yourselves in them” [al-Tawbah 9:36].

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah said, from Ibn ʿAbbās, on this verse, “so do not wrong yourselves in them”: In all of them. Then He singled out four of the months, made them sacred and their sanctity great, and made sin in them graver and righteous deeds and their reward greater.

Qatādah said of this verse: Know that wrongdoing in the sacred months is a graver sin and burden than at other times, even though wrongdoing is in every case a worthless thing; but Allah the Exalted magnifies whatever of His affair He wills, exalted is our Lord.
It has been narrated in two marfūʿ hadiths that bad deeds are multiplied in Ramaḍān, but their chains are not authentic.
Allah the Exalted says: “The Ḥajj is in well-known months; whoever undertakes the Ḥajj in them, let there be no intimacy, no wickedness and no quarrelling during the Ḥajj” [al-Baqarah 2:197].

Ibn ʿUmar said: Wickedness (fusūq) is any act of disobedience to Allah that is committed, whether hunting game or anything else. It is also reported from him that he said: Wickedness is committing acts of disobedience to Allah in the Sanctuary.
And the Exalted says: “And whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment” [al-Ḥajj 22:25].

A number of the Companions avoided living in the Sanctuary for fear of committing sins in it, among them Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz did likewise. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ used to say: A sin there is graver.
It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: That I should commit seventy sins — meaning outside Makkah — is dearer to me than that I should commit a single sin in Makkah.
From Mujāhid, who said: Bad deeds are multiplied in Makkah as good deeds are multiplied.
Ibn Jurayj said: It has reached me that a sin in Makkah counts as a hundred sins, and a good deed likewise.
Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr said: I said to Aḥmad: Is there anything in the hadiths saying that a bad deed is written as more than one?
He said: No; we have heard of nothing except at Makkah, because of the sanctity of the city: “Even if a man in ʿAdan Abyan intended…”
Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said as Aḥmad said. His words, “Even if a man in ʿAdan Abyan intended…”, are the words of Ibn Masʿūd, which we shall mention later, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Bad deeds may also be multiplied because of the eminence of the one who commits them, the strength of his knowledge of Allah and his nearness to Him; for whoever disobeys the sultan on his very carpet commits a graver crime than one who disobeys him from afar. That is why Allah has threatened His special servants with a doubled recompense for disobedience,

even though He has protected them from it, so as to show them His favour upon them in protecting them from it, as the Exalted says: “And had We not made you firm, you would almost have inclined to them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double in death” [al-Isrāʾ 17:74–75].

And the Exalted says: “O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a manifest indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her twofold, and that is easy for Allah. And whoever of you is devoutly obedient to Allah and His Messenger and does righteousness, We shall give her a twofold reward” [al-Aḥzāb 33:30–31].
ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn used to apply the like of this to the family of the Prophet ﷺ from Banū Hāshim, because of their nearness to the Prophet ﷺ.

The third kind is intending good deeds. A complete good deed is written, even if one does not do it, as in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās and others. In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah that Muslim recorded, as given above:
“When My servant talks of doing a good deed, I write it for him as a good deed.” The apparent meaning of this talking is talking to oneself, which is intending. In the hadith of Khuraym ibn Fātik:

“Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it” — and Allah knows that he has let his heart feel it and was eager for it — “a good deed is written for him.” This shows that what is meant by intending here
is the firm resolve that is accompanied by eagerness to act, not a mere passing thought that occurs and then dissolves without resolve or determination.
Abū al-Dardāʾ said: Whoever goes to his bed intending to pray during the night, and his eyes overcome him until morning, what he intended is written for him.
It has also been narrated from him as marfūʿ,
and Ibn Mājah recorded it as marfūʿ.
Al-Dāraquṭnī said: The mawqūf version is the well-preserved one. Its meaning has also been narrated from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, from the Prophet ﷺ.

It is narrated that Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: Whoever intends to pray, fast, perform Ḥajj or ʿUmrah, or go on campaign, and is prevented from it, Allah the Exalted will bring him to what he intended.
Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī said: The angel is called: Write for so-and-so such-and-such. He says: My Lord, he did not do it. And He says: He intended it.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: There was a man who used to go round the scholars saying: Who will direct me to a deed that will keep me always working for Allah? For I would not like any hour of the night or day to pass over me without my working for Allah the Exalted.
He was told: You have found what you need. Do good as much as you can, and when you grow weary or leave it, intend to do it; for one who intends to do good is like one who does it.

Whenever intention is joined by speech or effort, the recompense is confirmed and the person is counted with the one who acts, as Abū Kabshah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “This world belongs to four people. A servant whom Allah has provided with wealth and knowledge,

and he fears his Lord in it, maintains his ties of kinship with it, and knows that Allah has a right in it: he is in the best of stations. A servant whom Allah has provided with knowledge but not wealth, and he is sincere in intention, saying: If I had wealth, I would do as so-and-so does:

he has his intention, and their reward is the same. A servant whom Allah has provided with wealth but not knowledge, who blunders about in his wealth without knowledge, not fearing his Lord in it, not maintaining his ties of kinship with it, and not knowing that Allah has a right in it:

he is in the vilest of stations. And a servant whom Allah has provided with neither wealth nor knowledge, and he says: If I had wealth, I would do in it as so-and-so does: he has his intention, and their burden of sin is the same.” Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī — and this is his wording — and Ibn Mājah recorded it.

His words, “So they are equal in reward,” have been understood to mean that they are equal in the basic reward of the deed, not in its multiplication. The multiplication belongs only to the one who did the deed, not to the one who intended it but did not do it; for if they were equal in every respect,

ten good deeds would be written for whoever intended a good deed and did not do it, which is contrary to all the texts. This is shown by His words, Exalted is He: “Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind by a degree; and to each Allah has promised the best. But Allah has preferred those who strive above those who stay behind with a great reward — degrees from Him” [al-Nisāʾ 4:95–96].

Ibn ʿAbbās and others said: Those who stay behind, above whom the strivers are preferred by one degree, are those who stay behind with an excuse; and those who stay behind, above whom the strivers are preferred by degrees, are those who stay behind without an excuse.

The fourth kind is intending bad deeds without doing them. In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās such a deed is written as a complete good deed, and likewise in the hadiths of Abū Hurayrah, Anas and others it is written as a good deed. In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah he said: “He left it only min jarrāya” — that is, for My sake.
This shows that what is meant is someone who was able to commit the sin he intended and left it for the sake of Allah the Exalted. There is no doubt that a good deed is written for him for that,
because his leaving the sin with this aim is a righteous deed.
But if he intended a sin and then refrained from it out of fear of created beings, or to show off to them, it has been said that he is punished for refraining with this intention,
because putting fear of created beings before fear of Allah is unlawful.

Likewise, aiming to show off to created beings is unlawful; so when refraining from the sin is joined to it and done for its sake, he is punished for this refraining. Abū Nuʿaym recorded with a weak chain from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: You who commit sin, do not feel safe from its evil outcome;

what follows the sin is greater than the sin itself when you commit it. He said more, and said: Your fearing the wind when it stirs your door-curtain while you are in the midst of the sin, while your heart does not tremble at Allah's gaze upon you, is greater than the sin when you commit it.
Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: They used to say: Leaving a deed for the sake of people is showing off, and doing it for them is shirk.

But if he strove to bring it about as far as he could, and then decree came between him and it, a number of scholars have said that he is then punished for it, because of the words of the Prophet ﷺ: “Allah has pardoned my nation for what their souls whisper to them,
so long as they do not speak of it or act on it”; and whoever strives with all his effort to commit a sin and then is unable to has acted on it.

Likewise there are the words of the Prophet ﷺ: “When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire.” They said: Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, but what about the one killed?
He said: “He was eager to kill his companion.”
His words, “so long as they do not speak of it or act on it,” show that if one who intends a sin speaks with his tongue of what he intends, he is then punished for the intention,

because he has committed a sin with his limbs, namely speaking with his tongue. This is shown by the hadith of the man who said, “If I had wealth, I would do with it what so-and-so does” — meaning the one who disobeys Allah with his wealth — where he said: “So they are equal in the burden of sin.”
Some later scholars said: He is not punished for speaking of what he intends unless the sin he intended is an unlawful utterance, such as slander, backbiting or lying;

as for a sin that consists in action with the limbs, he does not sin merely by speaking of what he intends. The hadith of Abū Hurayrah given above may be cited for this: “And when My servant talks of doing a bad deed, I forgive it for him so long as he has not done it.”

But what is meant by talking in the hadith here is talking to oneself, so as to reconcile it with his words, “so long as they do not speak of it or act on it.” The hadith of Abū Kabshah shows this explicitly, for when someone says with his tongue, “If I had wealth, I would commit sins with it,

as so-and-so does,” that is not committing the sin he intended. He is only telling of what he intends, which concerns spending wealth on sins, while he has no wealth at all. Moreover, speaking in this way is itself unlawful, so how could it be pardoned and go unpunished?
But if his intention dissolves and his resolve weakens without any cause on his part, is he punished for the sin he intended or not?
This falls into two categories.

The first is where the intention to sin is a passing thought that occurred, which its owner did not dwell on or set his heart upon, but rather disliked and shrank from. This is pardoned; it is like the evil whisperings about which the Prophet ﷺ was asked, and he said: “That is pure faith.”

When His words, Exalted is He, came down — “Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it; then He will forgive whom He wills and punish whom He wills” [al-Baqarah 2:284] —

it weighed heavily on the Muslims, and they thought that these passing thoughts were included in it. So the verse after it came down, which includes His words: “Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear” [al-Baqarah 2:286].
This made clear that what they have no strength to bear is not held against them and is not something they are charged with. Ibn ʿAbbās and others called that abrogation,

and what they meant is that this verse removed the misapprehension that the first verse had caused in people's minds, and made clear that what is meant by the first verse is firm resolves. The Salaf used to call something like this abrogation.
The second category is firm resolves that occur in the soul and persist, on which their owner dwells. This too is of two types.

The first is what is an act of the heart in its own right, such as doubt about the divine oneness, or prophethood, or the resurrection, or any other form of disbelief and hypocrisy, or believing these to be false. For all of this the servant is punished, and by it he becomes a disbeliever or a hypocrite.

It is narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās understood His words, Exalted is He, “Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it” [al-Baqarah 2:284], as referring to things like this.
It is also narrated from him that he understood it as referring to concealing testimony, because of His words, Exalted is He: “And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful” [al-Baqarah 2:283].

Joined to this category are all the other sins that pertain to hearts, such as loving what Allah hates and hating what Allah loves, arrogance, self-admiration, envy, and thinking ill of a Muslim without cause;
though it is narrated that Sufyān said of thinking ill of others that, if no word or deed results from it, it is pardoned.

Something similar is narrated from al-Ḥasan about envy. Perhaps what the two of them said is to be understood of what a person finds in himself and cannot push away, so that he dislikes it and pushes it from himself, and yet it will not go away — not of what he dwells on and takes comfort in, turning it over again and again in his mind.

The printed text reads فلا يندفع إلاَّ على ما يساكنه, which contradicts the sense; read ولا يندفع، لا على ما يساكنه (“and yet it will not go away — not of what he dwells on”), as in the Abū al-Nūr edition and in al-Safārīnī's quotation of this passage in Ghidhāʾ al-Albāb. The Arnaʾūṭ edition shares the al-Faḥl reading.

The second type is what is not among the acts of hearts but among the acts of the limbs, such as fornication, theft, drinking wine, killing, slander and the like, when the servant persists in wanting it and resolving on it, though no trace of it has appeared outwardly at all.
On whether one is held to account for this, scholars have two well-known views.
The first is that one is held to account for it. Ibn al-Mubārak said: I asked Sufyān al-Thawrī: Is a servant held to account for an intention?
He said: If it is a resolve, he is held to account.
Many jurists, hadith scholars and theologians, of our [Ḥanbalī] school and others, preferred this view, citing for it such words of His, Mighty and Majestic is He, as

“And know that Allah knows what is within yourselves, so beware of Him” [al-Baqarah 2:235], and His words, “But He will hold you to account for what your hearts have earned” [al-Baqarah 2:225]; and such words of the Prophet ﷺ as
“Sin is what wavers in your breast and you would hate people to see.” They understood his words ﷺ, “Allah has pardoned my nation for what their souls whisper to them,

so long as they do not speak of it or act on it,” as referring to passing thoughts, and said: What the servant dwells on and sets his heart upon is part of what he earns and does, so it is not pardoned.
Some of them said that he is punished for it in this world with worries and griefs. This is narrated from ʿĀʾishah as marfūʿ and as mawqūf, but its authenticity is open to question.

It has also been said that the servant is brought to account for it on the Day of Resurrection: Allah makes him stand before it, then pardons him and does not punish him for it, so that his punishment is the reckoning itself. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas,

and it is the choice of Ibn Jarīr, who argued for it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar on the private conversation (al-najwā). But that hadith has no general sense; moreover, it concerns sins that were veiled in this world, not the whisperings of breasts.

The second view is that one is not held to account for mere intention at all. This has been attributed to an explicit statement of al-Shāfiʿī, and it is the view of Ibn Ḥāmid of our school, acting on the general texts.
Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās something that indicates a view like this.

There is a third view: that one is not held to account for intending a sin unless he intends to commit it in the Sanctuary, as al-Suddī reported from Murrah, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, who said: There is no servant who intends a sin

and does not do it that has it written against him — but if he intends to kill a man at the House while he is in ʿAdan Abyan, Allah will make him taste a painful punishment. And ʿAbdullāh recited: “And whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment” [al-Ḥajj 22:25].
Imam Aḥmad and others recorded it.
Shuʿbah and Sufyān reported it from al-Suddī: Shuʿbah gave it as marfūʿ and Sufyān as mawqūf, and Sufyān's position, that it is mawqūf, is the correct one.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: A man may intend a sin in Makkah while he is in another land, and it is written against him though he has not done it. Something indicating a view like this has already been given from Aḥmad and Isḥāq, and al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā likewise related it from Aḥmad.
In the narration of al-Marrūdhī, Aḥmad reported this hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, then said: He says, “whoever intends in it deviation through wrongdoing.” Aḥmad said:

If a man in ʿAdan Abyan intended to kill a man in the Sanctuary — this is the word of Allah, Glorified is He: “We shall make him taste a painful punishment.” That is what Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah have mercy on him) said.

Some referred this back to the sins that pertain to the heart, mentioned above, saying: The Sanctuary must be respected and revered in the heart, so the punishment is for neglecting this obligation. This is not correct, for the sanctity of the Sanctuary is not greater than the sanctity of the One who made it sacred, Glorified is He,

and resolving to disobey Allah is resolving to violate what He has made sacred. But if he resolved on it with the aim of violating the sanctity of the Sanctuary and out of contempt for its sanctity, that is like resolving to commit a sin with the aim of showing contempt for the sanctity of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic,

and by that he becomes a disbeliever. Disbelief is ruled out for him only when his intending the sin is merely to satisfy his desire and his own aim, while he is heedless of any intention to defy Allah or to show contempt for His majesty and His gaze. Whenever an act is joined to the intention, he is punished for it,

whether the act comes after it or before it. Whoever commits something unlawful once and then resolves to do it whenever he is able persists in sin and is punished for this intention, even if he does not go back to doing it for many years.
That is how Ibn al-Mubārak and others explained persistence in sin.

In any case, a sin is written only as one like it, without multiplication. The punishment is for the sin, and the intention to commit it is not added to it; for if the intention were added to the sin, one would be punished twice for committing a sin. It cannot be said that the same must then hold for doing a good deed,

so that when one does it after intending it, one is rewarded for the good deed but not for the intention; for we say that this is not conceded. Whoever does a good deed has ten like it written for him, so some of these ten may be the recompense for intending the good deed. And Allah knows best.

His words in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, in the narration of Muslim, “or Allah erases it,” mean that when a bad deed is done, either a single bad deed is written for the one who did it, or Allah erases it by whatever means He wills, such as repentance, seeking forgiveness and doing good deeds.
What bad deeds are erased by has already been discussed in the commentary on the hadith of Abū Dharr: “Fear Allah wherever you are, and follow a bad deed with a good one and it will erase it.”
His words after that, “and none perishes before Allah except one who is doomed to perish,” mean that after this great bounty from Allah and His vast mercy, in multiplying good deeds

and overlooking bad deeds, none perishes before Allah except one who has brought about his own ruin, thrown himself into destruction with his own hands, made bold to commit bad deeds, and shunned good deeds and turned away from them.
That is why Ibn Masʿūd said: Woe to the one whose ones outnumber his tens.
Al-Kalbī reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, as marfūʿ: “Ruined is he whose one outweighs ten.”
Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“There are two practices which no Muslim man keeps up without entering Paradise; they are easy, but those who do them are few. You glorify Allah after every prayer ten times,

praise Him ten times and magnify Him ten times.” He said: “That makes a hundred and fifty on the tongue and one thousand five hundred in the Balance. And when you go to bed, you glorify Him, magnify Him and praise Him a hundred times: that is a hundred on the tongue and a thousand in the Balance. So which of you does two thousand five hundred bad deeds in a day and a night?”
In the Musnad, from Abū al-Dardāʾ, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Let none of you fail to do a thousand good deeds for Allah each morning, by saying

subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi a hundred times, for that is a thousand good deeds. If Allah the Exalted wills, he will not commit as many sins as that in his day, and whatever other good he does will be a surplus.”
